question: The Lisbon Treaty strengthened the role of the regions in the creation of EU legislation, highlighting the importance of regional autonomy as part of the constitutional identity of Member States1 and promoting representative democracy closer to the citizens2. This begs the question as to whether Sicily is genuinely involved in the EU decision-making process.

The Protocol on the principles of subsidiarity and proportionality encourages extensive consultations3, involving the regions, while Regional Law No 234/2012 details the arrangements for regional participation in the EU, with a reference to the active engagement of the Sicilian Regional Assembly (ARS).
Regional Law No 10/2010 lays emphasis on the role of the regional government in representing Sicily in respect of EU proposals.

However, the failure to implement this law has hampered Assembly-Government cooperation in creating EU policies, thus pointing to the need for a legislative update post-Lisbon Treaty and Law No 234/2012, which transformed Italian participation in the EU, and emphasising the importance of the bottom-up approach and the State-Regions Conference for regional engagement4.
In the light of the above, can the Commission state: 1.
How it views the participation of Sicily, and in particular the Sicilian Regional Assembly, in the process of moulding EU legislation and policies, with reference to the TEU and Law No 234/2012?
What measures it will promote to ensure compliance with the principles of subsidiarity and proximity in relations between the EU, Italy and Sicily?
How the link between the Regional Government and the Sicilian Regional Assembly can be improved so as to strengthen Sicily’s participation in the EU decision-making process?

Article 4(2) TEU. Article 10(1) and (3) TEU. answer: 1. Article 6 of Protocol No 2 on the application of the principles of subsidiarity and proportionality sets out that regional parliaments with legislative powers should be consulted, where appropriate, by their national parliament when the latter examine an EU draft legislative act for its compliance with the principle of subsidiarity.

The Commission is not aware of how often and to what extent this stipulation has been put in practice with the involvement of the Sicilian Regional Assembly, and it cannot comment on the national constitutional and political setup defining the interplay between the national parliament and regional parliaments in the Member States. 2.

The Commission systematically applies the principles of subsidiarity and proportionality to its legislative proposals as part of its better regulation agenda and toolbox (5). It attaches a subsidiarity assessment grid to all politically sensitive and important proposals accompanied by an impact assessment.

In this context, the Commission encourages regional parliaments to participate in its public consultations, submitting their views and regional evidence at the early stage of the preparation of proposals. 3. The Commission cannot take position on the relations between a regional government and a regional assembly.

It notes that regional parliaments and governments are represented in the European Committee of the Regions and interact with the Commission via the Committee. Regional parliaments also transmit their views on Commission initiatives via the Conference of European Regional Legislative Assemblies (CALRE).
